analysis.one_liner: Sets federal minimum safety rules for sports betting, including deposit limits and a credit-card betting ban.
analysis.headline: A lone House member's bill to impose federal safety standards on sports betting has sat in committee with zero cosponsors and no action since March 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make sports betting legal only in states whose programs win Justice Department approval every three years. Approved programs would have to meet minimum standards: no betting under 21, no deposits by credit card, limits on how much a person can deposit before an income check, a ban on ads during live sports, no bonuses or VIP rewards tied to gambling activity, a national self-exclusion list for people who want to block themselves, and operator funding for gambling-addiction treatment. It also directs federal health agencies to track gambling addiction nationwide and requires a Surgeon General's report on the public health effects of widespread sports betting.
analysis.who_benefits: People who bet on sports and people at risk of gambling addiction. The bill would stop operators from letting customers fund bets with credit cards, cap deposits at five per day, require income checks before large deposits, ban ads during live games and daytime broadcasts, outlaw bonus offers and VIP programs that reward heavy gambling, and bar the use of AI to target individual bettors with promotions. Anyone who wants to stop betting could put themselves on a national self-exclusion list that all operators must honor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Sports bettors and people at risk of gambling addiction

how_it_helps.text: Operators could not accept deposits made with a credit card, could take no more than five deposits per person per day, and would have to verify income before accepting more than $1,000 in a day or $10,000 in 30 days [S3].

Operators could not offer reload bonuses, tiered rewards, or VIP perks tied to how much a customer gambles, and could not use artificial intelligence to track an individual's wagers or create targeted promotions [S3].
States would have to run a self-exclusion list coordinated with a national list, and operators could not accept bets from anyone under 21 or from anyone on those lists [S3].

Operators would have to dedicate a share of revenue to treatment for gambling disorder and education, and federal agencies would run an annual nationwide survey of online betting harms, build a gambling-addiction surveillance system, and produce a Surgeon General's report [S2] [S3].
Sports betting ads could not air during live game broadcasts or between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m., and marketing could not target problem gamblers, minors, or use odds-boost offers [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Online sports betting companies and casinos, which would lose marketing tools, bonus programs, AI-driven customer targeting, credit-card deposits, and unrestricted bet sizes — major revenue drivers. States would also cede some control: their programs would need Justice Department approval every three years and would have to meet federal standards on top of their own. Some bettors would face added friction, including income verification for larger deposits and collection of detailed personal records.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sports betting operators, casinos, and state programs

drawbacks.text: The bill would insert the federal government into gambling regulation that states have run since a 2018 Supreme Court decision opened the door to legal sports betting, requiring Justice Department approval and renewal every three years and creating a period of legal uncertainty, since unapproved programs would be barred [S3].

It requires operators to collect and keep sensitive personal data — names, addresses, Social Security or passport numbers, and the details of every wager — for at least five years, raising privacy and data-security concerns even though the bill also mandates data-security safeguards [S3].

Honest supporters would acknowledge the cost: advertising bans during live sports and daytime hours would cut broadcaster and league advertising revenue, and the licensing suitability rules could disqualify some existing operators outright, which would concentrate the market among the few companies able to clear the background-check bar [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections target practices specifically designed to keep people betting past what they can afford — credit-card deposits, reload bonuses, VIP programs, AI-targeted promotions — and the addiction-tracking provisions would for the first time give the country real data on gambling harm. The main tradeoffs are a heavier compliance burden on operators, more federal control over state-run programs, and collection of detailed personal betting records by private companies. For people who gamble, the restrictions cut against convenience but directly against the mechanics of problem gambling.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in March 2025 and referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no cosponsors, no hearings scheduled, and no further action.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on March 11, 2025; it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Natural Resources Committee [S1] [S5].
No other member has cosponsored it [S4], and the committees have taken no action since referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, online sports betting operators, who continue to run under state rules only, with no federal restrictions on credit-card deposits, targeted promotions, or live-game advertising.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online sports betting operators, for now

for.name: Rep. Paul Tonko
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor; introduced the bill on March 11, 2025.

against.name: Sports betting industry (DraftKings, FanDuel, MGM and similar operators)
against.what_they_did: The bill has drawn no cosponsors and has not advanced past committee referral; industry groups publicly opposed comparable federal gambling restrictions when Tonko first introduced them in the prior Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have been taken and no cosponsors have joined, so the partisan shape of support and opposition is unknown.

industries.note: Operators would lose some of their most effective revenue tools: credit-card deposits, reload bonuses, VIP rewards, AI-targeted promotions, and daytime and live-game advertising, plus they would face affordability checks on large deposits. The public-health rationale is that these tools drive problem gambling losses that fall on ordinary households.

State and tribal programs would have to win Justice Department approval every three years and meet federal standards, adding compliance costs. The bill does preserve tribal authority over servers on Indian lands and leaves state taxation untouched.

Leagues would gain tools to restrict betting on their events and get suspicious-transaction reports, and they would remain a licensed data source for settling wagers. Broadcasters would lose advertising slots, since sports-betting ads could not run during live games or between 8 a.m. and 10 p.m.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors, no committee hearings, and no movement since its March 2025 referral, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress; most bills stuck this long at this stage die when the session ends.
